title: Which of sync interval, compression, delay, momentum and robust aggregation sets the final loss of low-communication training?
lede: research programme (milestone 6, results on small transformers): a predictive theory of DiLoCo-style low-communication training, testing on real small transformers the closed forms derived in about a dozen quadratic-model projects, with 16 references, hypotheses H1 to H6 and an ICML/NeurIPS workshop as the first target
summary: An open research programme rather than a finished project. DiLoCo-style training cuts communication by orders of magnitude, but choosing the sync interval, compressor and outer optimiser is still a sweep at every scale, and the best empirical scaling laws do not say why one axis costs more than another. This repository holds about a dozen closed-form results on a quadratic with gradient noise (a noise floor inflated by 1+ω under compression, a delay stability limit 2 sin(π/(4τ+2)), an optimal outer momentum that falls with the sync interval, a median that costs π/2 in variance). The programme asks whether those structural factors survive on trained transformers and compose, so that two or three measured constants per model size predict the final loss of configurations never run, as well as a refitted scaling law does. Six falsifiable hypotheses each state the result that would refute them. Milestone 1 is done: a simulated M-worker DiLoCo harness on a 0.41M-parameter GPT reproduces the synchronous loop exactly at M=1, H=1 and the quadratic closed form to 2% (ratio 0.983, 95% CI containing it). Since then, milestones 3 to 6 tested the hypotheses on a 0.41M- and a 0.92M-parameter GPT: DiLoCo at H=16 beats synchronous AdamW by 0.012 nats over 11 seeds; rand-k compression costs in proportion to ω at H=16 but is free up to ω about 8 at H=64, with H=32 in between (the cost is a function of ω and H jointly); error-feedback top-k is free to keep 1/16. Milestone 6u refuted the leading explanation for that knee: the rand-k noise per unit of ω, measured against the workers' own disagreement, is the same at every H to within 3% (E/V 1.07, 1.08, 1.11). Milestone 6v ruled out rand-k’s sparsity too: Gaussian noise with rand-k’s per-coordinate variance and nothing dropped is free at H=64 and costs at H=16, like rand-k. 6w ruled out a contraction mechanism: one round of rand-k noise injected at mid-training keeps all its parameter-space energy over 256 inner steps at both H, and its loss cost is larger at H=64 (+0.012 nats) than at H=16 (+0.006), so single-round costs do not add up to the run’s cost. 6x split the run’s cost by forking at the last round: every round of keep-1/8 noise costs about the same when injected (+0.012 nats at H=64, +0.006 at H=16, with no adaptation in compressed runs), and the trajectory before the last round is worse than uncompressed at H=16 (+0.016) but better at H=64 (−0.014, all four seeds). So “free” compression at H=64 is a training gain cancelling the last round’s cost, and sending only the last sync uncompressed beats uncompressed training there. 6y checked the baseline: plain averaging (outer SGD lr 1) beat outer lr 0.7, 1.5, 2 and Nesterov momentum for uncompressed training, and the uncompressed-last-round recipe still ended 0.014 nats below it on 64 validation batches no earlier step had read (2.2 se, three of four seeds), so the gain is not an under-tuned baseline. A larger outer step reached the recipe’s weight norm and ended 0.05 nats worse, so the gain is not larger weights either. 6z mapped the recipe across compression levels: on the fresh batches it ends −0.018 nats against uncompressed at keep 1/4 (all four seeds), −0.014 at keep 1/8, −0.014 with Gaussian noise of rand-k’s per-coordinate variance and nothing dropped, +0.011 at keep 1/16 and +0.081 at keep 1/32, so the gain comes from outer-step noise rather than sparsity and is largest at the smallest compression tried, while the last sync’s own cost is close to linear in ω. 6aa placed the optimum: the gain is about zero at ω=1/3, −0.012 (rand-k) and −0.007 (Gaussian) at ω=1 and largest at ω=3 (−0.018 with either noise), so keep 1/4 is the setting to use here; keep 1/2 sends twice the bytes for about half the gain (pooled over the two noises, keep 1/4 wins by 0.009 nats, 3.9 se, exploratory; the registered omega-1 tests fell just short of 2 se). The last sync’s cost is linear in ω from 1/3 to 31. 6ab ran the recipe at H=16: keep 1/4 with a dense last sync lands within 0.001 nats of uncompressed (se 0.0035) and keep 1/8 costs 0.014 (3.9 se), so the gain is an H=64 effect, and at short sync intervals compression is at best free. 6ac ran H=32: keep 1/2, 1/4 and 1/8 with a dense last sync end +0.001, −0.006 and +0.002 nats against uncompressed (se 0.005 to 0.009), between the H=16 and H=64 values but within noise of zero, and the last sync’s cost per unit of ω already matches H=64. 6ad added seeds 4 to 7: pooled over eight seeds keep 1/4 ends −0.0072 nats (se 0.0041, 7 of 8 seeds below zero) and keep 1/8 +0.003, so keep 1/4 with a dense last sync is at or below uncompressed at every H tried, and the gain at H=32 is small and not yet resolved. 6ae gave the headline H=64 cell eight seeds: keep 1/4 with a dense last sync ends −0.0134 nats below uncompressed (se 0.0026, 7 of 8 seeds, exact sign-flip P=0.016), smaller than the first four seeds’ −0.0185. A paper section (paper/section_recipe.md) draws milestones 6w to 6ae together. Results are on a character-level Shakespeare model on CPU; the research log has every pre-registered hypothesis, held or refuted.
